# Cūḷanandiyajātaka (Ja 222)
**ID:** Ja 222
**Section:** Jātaka (ja)

## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Cūḷanandiyajātaka* (Ja 222), rendered as *The Monkey Nandiya*, is a canonical Pali Jātaka tale belonging to the Jātaka collection [SuttaCentral]. According to the commentary and framing narrative, the Buddha delivered this discourse while residing at the Bamboo Grove (Veḷuvana) in Rājagaha concerning Devadatta, occasioned by a discussion among monks regarding Devadatta's fierce, violent disposition and his attempts on the Buddha's life [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879].
The tale exemplifies the karmic law of actions and their consequences, encapsulated in the teaching that as one sows, so one reaps—reaping good from good deeds and evil from evil deeds [Sarao and Long 2017].
Curated parallels recorded on SuttaCentral identify a passage-level parallel in the *Venasākhajātaka* (Ja 353), and note that the text is referenced in the *Peṭakopadesa* (Pe 2, *Sāsanapaṭṭhānadutiyabhūmi*) [SuttaCentral]. Text-reuse analysis by DharmaNexus confirms the Pali-internal relationship with the *Venasākhajātaka* (Ja 353), finding substantial overlap between segment §1.4–2.6 and Ja 353 §2.1–2.6, in addition to extensive textual alignments with the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* [DharmaNexus].
